pendent (Fig. 3). GRSs are typically composed of hundreds to millions of genetic variants which can be combined in several
ways: unweighted and weighted. In weighted GRSs, we use a weighted sum of allele dosages multiplied by their corresponding effect
sizes, as estimated from a relevant GWAS. In unweighted GRSs only the sum of the number of risk alleles contributed by each SNP
included in the GRS is taken into account. However, the use of unweighted GRSs has the disadvantage that it does not take into
account the magnitude of the association with the phenotype of interest for each of the SNPs included in the GRS, since the presence
of each risk allele in the GRS scores the same regardless of whether it is an SNP highly associated with the risk phenotype or whether
the association is 5 or 10 times smaller. Currently, there has become available a great resource from the EMBL, called PGS Catalog,
that gathers all published GRSs consistently annotated with relevant metadata; including scoring ﬁles (variants, effect alleles/
weights), annotations of how the PGS was developed and applied, and evaluations of their predictive performance. These GRS,
both weighted and unweighted, are used as variables measuring genetic susceptibility in subsequent statistical analyses of gene-
diet interactions.
